page_title: Don’t start with microservices in production – monoliths are your friend

sources.entry: Don’t start with microservices in production – monoliths are your friend

summary.title: Don't start with microservices in production – monoliths are your friend
summary.one_liner: Starting a brand-new project with microservices adds heavy infrastructure, deployment, organizational and error-handling costs that often outweigh their promised benefits, so a monolith is frequently the better first choice.
takeaways: Microservices bring real benefits (fault isolation, independent deployment, per-service scaling, tech diversity) but only if the team works hard to achieve them.
Microservices need much more infrastructure (Kubernetes, messaging, tracing, monitoring) than a monolith, increasing cost and failure points.
Decomposing a product into too many small services can make single features span many services and slow deployments down.
Distributed error handling (timeouts, failures propagating across services) is much harder than a try-catch in a monolith.
The author's experience suggests starting with a monolith, with the chapter 2 follow-up discussing the counterpart.
summary.summary: The author argues against starting a greenfield project with microservices, drawing on first-hand experience. He goes through the usual advantages (fault isolation, avoiding technology lock-in, easier understanding, faster deployment, scalability) and explains why each is hard to realize in practice. He compares the infrastructure footprint of a simple monolith with a microservice setup (Kubernetes, messaging, Prometheus, tracing), describes a project that ended with 80+ services and slower deployments, and illustrates how cross-service failures cascade without proper error handling. The post is an opinion piece based on anecdotes rather than benchmarks, and it ends with a promise of a second part.
